item.title: pricing-models-ri-savings-plans-spot
item.description:
Pricing Models: On-Demand, RIs, Savings Plans and Spot#

Almost every cost question is a matching game: workload pattern → purchase option. Get these five into your head and half of Domain 4 is free.

The options#

Option Discount Commitment Best for
On-Demand 0% None Spiky, unknown, short-lived workloads
Savings Plans (Compute / EC2 Instance / SageMaker) up to 72% 1 or 3 years, $/hour commitment Steady usage, want flexibility
Reserved Instances (Standard / Convertible) up to 72% 1 or 3 years, specific instance family Very steady, known capacity
Spot Instances up to 90% None - can be reclaimed (2-min notice) Fault-tolerant, interruptible work
Dedicated Hosts / Instances 0% (premium) None/1-3y Licensing, compliance, single-tenant

Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances (a favorite comparison)#

  • Savings Plans = commit to $X/hour of compute; covers any instance family, region (Compute SP), Fargate and Lambda too. More flexible → usually the better answer
  • Reserved Instances = commit to a specific instance type/region; can be standard (most discount, resellable) or convertible (less discount, can change family/OS); zonal RI also reserves capacity in an AZ
  • Scheduled RIs = recurring time windows (rarely tested)

Not: “surekli calisan ve tahmin edilebilir is yuk” = Savings Plans (esnek oldugu icin RI’ye tercih edilir). “Kesintiye dayanikli toplu is / ML egitim / test ortami” = Spot. “Windows/SQL lisansi bizim” = Dedicated Host.

item.title: s3-cost-and-lifecycle-policies
item.description:
S3 Cost Optimization and Lifecycle Policies#

S3 cost questions are really about storage class transitions and data transfer - the two levers that move the bill the most.

Lifecycle policies - the main tool#

Two rule types:

  • Transition - move objects to cheaper classes over time (e.g. Standard → IA after 30 days → Glacier Instant after 90)
  • Expiration - delete objects/versions after N days

item.title: cost-management-tools
item.description:
Cost Management Tools#

“Which tool should the company use to see/track/limit spending?” - the answer is one of a small set of billing tools. Learn what each one uniquely does.

The lineup#

Tool What it’s for Scenario keyword
Cost Explorer Visualize & forecast costs, RI/SP utilization & coverage “why did costs rise”, “should we buy RIs”
Cost & Usage Report (CUR) Most granular billing data (hourly, resource-level) “detailed analysis in Athena/QuickSight”
Budgets Alert and act at thresholds “notify me at 80% of budget”, “stop resources”
Cost Anomaly Detection ML-based unusual-spend alerts “sudden unexpected spike”
Pricing Calculator Estimate costs before building “what will this architecture cost”
Trusted Advisor Best-practice checks: cost, security, performance, fault tolerance, service limits “find idle resources, unattached EBS”
Compute Optimizer Right-size recommendations “is this instance too big”
AWS Budgets + Billing Alarms Classic proactive control CloudWatch alarm on estimated charges

Details worth knowing#

  • Cost Explorer: 12 months history default, forecasting up to 12 months, save custom views; RI/SP utilization reports answer “are we wasting our commitment”
  • CUR is the only source with full resource-level detail → analyze with Athena, visualize with QuickSight
  • Budgets can trigger actions (e.g. apply an IAM policy via Service Catalog to stop non-prod); alert types: actual, forecasted, and planned (RI/SP)
  • Trusted Advisor full checks require Business/Enterprise support; the “cost” category finds idle ELBs, unassociated Elastic IPs, low-utilization instances
  • Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics and recommends right-sized instances (needs opt-in)
flowchart LR
    usage[AWS usage] --> ce[Cost Explorer: what happened?]
    usage --> cur[CUR: raw detail]
    usage --> budget[Budgets: alert/act]
    usage --> ta[Trusted Advisor: fix waste]
    usage --> co[Compute Optimizer: right-size]

Not: sinav eslesmeleri: “harcama gecmisi ve RI karari” = Cost Explorer, “en detayli veri” = CUR, “butce asiminda uyari/aksiyon” = Budgets, “bos kaynak / limit uyari” = Trusted Advisor, “instance fazla buyuk mu” = Compute Optimizer.

item.title: cost-optimized-architecture-patterns
item.description:
Cost-Optimized Architecture Patterns#

The last Domain 4 piece: not a tool, but a habit set. The exam’s “MOST cost-effective” questions are usually one of these patterns wearing a scenario costume.

The pattern checklist#

  1. Right-size - use Compute Optimizer; T-family burstables for spiky small work; don’t pay for a 16-vCPU box that idles at 5%
  2. Turn things off - dev/test schedules (Instance Scheduler), stop idle instances, delete unattached EBS volumes and idle ELBs (Trusted Advisor finds them)
  3. Pay for commitment, not flexibility - steady state → Savings Plans/RI; see pricing-models
  4. Embrace Spot and serverless - batch/CI/stateless → Spot; event-driven, spiky → Lambda/Fargate (pay per use, no idle)
  5. Right storage class + lifecycle - s3-cost-and-lifecycle-policies
  6. Cache to cut backend load - CloudFront + ElastiCache = fewer DB instances, less egress (also better perf)
  7. Route data cheaply - VPC gateway endpoints (free S3 access vs NAT charges), keep inter-service traffic in-region/AZ, CloudFront for internet egress
  8. S3 instead of compute - static hosting on S3/CloudFront beats an always-on web server

Cost-aware multi-tier design#

flowchart LR
    users[Users] --> cf[CloudFront - cached, cheap egress]
    cf --> alb[ALB]
    alb --> asg[ASG with Spot + On-Demand mix]
    asg --> sqs[SQS buffer]
    sqs --> lambda[Lambda consumers]
    asg & lambda --> ddb[DynamoDB on-demand]

Exam nuance: “most cost-effective” still must meet requirements. If the question says the workload is steady and latency-sensitive, Spot is wrong even though it’s cheapest. Cost answers are always “cheapest that works”.
